title: Cleaning blanks out of a name list
scenario: The loop should drop empty strings from the list and print what is left. Instead the program dies before printing anything.
symptom:
Exception in thread "main" java.util.ConcurrentModificationException
	at java.base/java.util.ArrayList$Itr.checkForComodification(ArrayList.java:1013)
	at java.base/java.util.ArrayList$Itr.next(ArrayList.java:967)
	at Main.main(Main.java:7)
question: What's the root cause?
options: List.of made the list immutable, so remove() is refused
The list shrinks inside a for-each; the iterator's next() sees modCount changed
remove(n) is resolved as remove(int index) and goes out of range
ArrayList is not thread-safe and the JIT reorders the removal
explanation: A for-each loop over an ArrayList uses its Iterator. names.remove(n) changes the list structurally behind the iterator's back, bumping modCount. On the next call to next(), checkForComodification() sees modCount != expectedModCount and throws. It is fail-fast behaviour in a single thread, not a race; the list was copied into an ArrayList, so it is mutable.
fixNote: Replaced the for-each + remove with names.removeIf(String::isEmpty) (Iterator.remove() in an explicit loop also works).
debugTip: Add an exception breakpoint on java.util.ConcurrentModificationException. When it hits, walk down the stack past the ArrayList$Itr frames to the first Main frame (line 7) and add a watch on names.size() while stepping the loop body.

title: The set forgets a point it already has
scenario: A path finder records visited points in a HashSet. Two points with the same coordinates are equal, yet the set claims it has never seen the second one and stores it again.
question: What's the root cause?
options: equals must take a Point parameter, not Object, to be used
The fields are final, so HashSet cannot read them
hashCode is not overridden, so equal points hash to different buckets
HashSet compares elements with ==, never with equals
explanation: HashSet first uses hashCode() to pick a bucket and only then calls equals() on entries with a matching hash. Point inherits Object.hashCode(), which is based on identity, so two equal points almost always have different hashes and equals() is never consulted. The contract says equal objects must have equal hash codes; override both together.
fixNote: Added hashCode() returning Objects.hash(x, y) to match equals().
debugTip: Break on line 21 and evaluate q.hashCode() and new Point(1, 2).hashCode() in the debugger: different values for equal objects immediately point at a missing hashCode().

title: The owner entry vanished from the map
scenario: Cells are keyed by their coordinate list. After the cell list grows, nobody can find "alice" any more, even by looking up [1, 2], yet the map still has one entry.
question: What's the root cause?
options: The key object was mutated after insertion, so its hash and equality changed
HashMap cannot use a List as a key; it needs a String
List.of(1, 2) and ArrayList are never equal to each other
get() needs the exact same reference that was used for put()
explanation: HashMap stores each entry in a bucket chosen from the key's hashCode() at put time. Adding 3 to the list changes its hashCode() and equals(), so get(cell) looks in a different bucket, and get(List.of(1, 2)) finds the right bucket but the stored key is now [1, 2, 3], which is not equal. The entry is still there (size 1) but unreachable. Keys must not change in ways that affect equals/hashCode while in a map.
fixNote: Store an immutable copy as the key: owner.put(List.copyOf(cell), "alice").
debugTip: Break on line 7 and evaluate cell.hashCode(), then step over line 8 and evaluate it again (994 vs 30817). A key whose hash changes after put() is the smoking gun.

title: Adding a colour to a ready-made list
scenario: The palette starts from an array and should gain one more colour. It prints the size and then crashes.
symptom:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException
	at java.base/java.util.AbstractList.add(AbstractList.java:153)
	at java.base/java.util.AbstractList.add(AbstractList.java:111)
	at Main.main(Main.java:8)
question: Why does add() fail here?
options: String arrays cannot be converted to lists of String
The list is immutable because base was declared with {}
add() needs an index when the list came from an array
Arrays.asList returns a fixed-size view backed by the array
explanation: Arrays.asList wraps the array in a fixed-size List (java.util.Arrays$ArrayList). It supports set() but not add() or remove(), which fall through to AbstractList's default implementations that throw UnsupportedOperationException. The AbstractList frames tell you the class did not override add().
fixNote: Copied into a growable list: new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(base)).
debugTip: Read the trace from the top until the first Main frame (line 8); the AbstractList.add frames mean the concrete list never implemented add. Evaluate colors.getClass() at a breakpoint to see java.util.Arrays$ArrayList.

title: Who changed the original array?
scenario: A list is made from an array, then each is edited separately. The author expected the two to be independent.
question: What does this print?
options: [z, b, c] then [a, b, y]
[z, b, y] then [z, b, y]
[z, b, c] then [z, b, y]
[z, b, y] then [a, b, y]
explanation: Arrays.asList does not copy: the returned list is a view that reads and writes the original array. view.set(0, "z") writes into base[0], and base[2] = "y" is visible through the list. Both lines show the same three elements.
fixNote: Wrapped in new ArrayList<>(...) so the list is an independent copy.
debugTip: Put a watch on both base[0] and view.get(0), then step over line 7: the array element changes too, proving the list is a write-through view.

title: Banning user 1 removes the wrong user
scenario: The code should remove the banned id 1 from the list. Instead id 20 disappears and 1 is still there.
question: What's the root cause?
options: remove(int) is chosen over remove(Object), so index 1 is removed
List.of copies values in reverse, so index 1 holds 20
remove() removes the first element greater than the argument
banned is autoboxed to a different Integer than the one stored
explanation: List has two overloads: remove(int index) and remove(Object o). With a primitive int argument, overload resolution picks remove(int) without boxing, so the element at index 1 (20) is removed. Pass an Integer to get remove(Object), which removes by equality.
fixNote: Call ids.remove(Integer.valueOf(banned)) so the remove(Object) overload is used.
debugTip: Use step into on line 8: the debugger lands in ArrayList.remove(int index), not remove(Object), which shows which overload the compiler chose.

title: Tied scores that are not tied
scenario: A leaderboard checks whether two players have the same score by comparing the values fetched from a map.
question: What does this print (default JVM settings)?
options: true then true
false then false
true then false
false then true
explanation: put("ann", 127) autoboxes with Integer.valueOf, which returns cached objects for -128..127, so a and b are the same object and == is true. 1000 is outside the cache, so each valueOf(1000) creates a new Integer and == compares two different references. Compare boxed values with equals() (or unbox to int).
fixNote: Compare the Integer values with equals() instead of ==.
debugTip: Break on line 12 and inspect c and d in the variables view: most debuggers show an object id per reference, and the two 1000s have different ids while the two 127s share one.

title: Stock report stops at the second item
scenario: Each ordered item should print its stock count, with unknown items counted as 0. The report prints one line and then crashes.
symptom:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "java.lang.Integer.intValue()" because the return value of "java.util.Map.get(Object)" is null
	at Main.main(Main.java:10)
question: What's the root cause?
options: stock itself is null because HashMap was never initialised
item is null for the second element of the array
HashMap.get throws when the key is missing
get returns null for "plum" and unboxing null into int throws
explanation: Map.get returns null for a missing key. Assigning that Integer to an int makes the compiler insert intValue(), and calling it on null throws NullPointerException. Java's helpful NPE message says exactly that: the return value of Map.get(Object) is null. Use getOrDefault or keep the value as Integer and check it.
fixNote: Used stock.getOrDefault(item, 0) so a missing item counts as 0.
debugTip: Set a conditional breakpoint on line 10 with condition !stock.containsKey(item); it stops exactly on "plum", where evaluating stock.get(item) shows null.

title: Sorting offsets leaves a big one last
scenario: Time offsets are sorted ascending. The result keeps the most negative offset at the end, and the sort raises no error.
question: What's the root cause?
options: List.sort is stable, so it keeps the original order of ties
a - b overflows int, so -2e9 vs 1e9 compares as positive
The lambda compares Integer references, not values
Underscores in numeric literals change their value
explanation: -2,000,000,000 - 1,000,000,000 is -3e9, which does not fit in an int and wraps around to +1,294,967,296. The comparator therefore says -2e9 is greater than 1e9, and TimSort sees the list as already ascending. Use Integer.compare (or Comparator.naturalOrder()), which never overflows.
fixNote: Replaced the subtraction comparator with Integer::compare.
debugTip: Put a breakpoint inside the lambda on line 7 and evaluate a - b alongside Integer.compare(a, b) for each call; the sign disagrees on the call with -2000000000 and 1000000000.

title: A head slice breaks after an append
scenario: The first three items are kept as a "head" slice. After a new item is appended to the full list, asking the slice for its size crashes.
symptom:
Exception in thread "main" java.util.ConcurrentModificationException
	at java.base/java.util.ArrayList$SubList.checkForComodification(ArrayList.java:1415)
	at java.base/java.util.ArrayList$SubList.size(ArrayList.java:1150)
	at Main.main(Main.java:10)
question: What's the root cause?
options: subList is a view; changing the parent structurally invalidates it
add(6) went past the subList range 0..3
Printing head on line 8 consumed its iterator
subList returns an immutable list, so size() is unsupported
explanation: ArrayList.subList returns a view that shares the parent's storage and remembers the parent's modCount. Any structural change made directly to the parent (add, remove, clear) makes the view's state undefined, and ArrayList's SubList detects it and throws ConcurrentModificationException on the next access. Copy the slice if it must outlive changes to the parent.
fixNote: Copied the slice with new ArrayList<>(all.subList(0, 3)).
debugTip: The trace shows a CME with no loop in sight; the ArrayList$SubList frames reveal it is the view, not an iterator. Set an exception breakpoint on ConcurrentModificationException and inspect head.getClass() to confirm it is a SubList.

title: Ranking the top three reorders everyone
scenario: The first three scores are sorted for a podium display. The full score list was supposed to stay in arrival order.
question: What does this print?
explanation: subList returns a view over positions 0..2 of scores, not a copy. Sorting the view writes the sorted elements back into those positions of the parent list. Only the first three slots change; 20 and 50 are outside the view and stay put.
fixNote: Sorted a copy: new ArrayList<>(scores.subList(0, 3)).
debugTip: Add a watch on scores and step over line 8; the watch changes even though only top was sorted, which shows top is a view.

title: A team member silently goes missing
scenario: Employees are kept in a TreeSet ordered by age. Three people are added but only two are in the set, and no error is raised.
question: What's the root cause?
options: Records cannot be stored in a TreeSet without implementing Comparable
TreeSet keeps only the first 2 elements until it is rebalanced
The comparator returns 0 for ann and cat, so TreeSet treats them as duplicates
Records generate equals() that only compares the first field
explanation: A TreeSet decides uniqueness with its comparator, not with equals(). comparingInt(Emp::age) returns 0 for any two 30-year-olds, so add(cat) finds an "equal" element and returns false. The comparator should be consistent with equals: break ties on another field.
fixNote: Added .thenComparing(Emp::name) so only truly equal employees compare as 0.
debugTip: Evaluate team.add(new Emp("cat", 30)) in the debugger at line 12 and see it return false; then evaluate byAge.compare(new Emp("ann", 30), new Emp("cat", 30)) to get 0.

title: The snapshot keeps changing
scenario: A read-only snapshot of the version list is taken before a new version is added. The snapshot should still show one version, but it shows two.
question: What's the root cause?
options: unmodifiableList copies lazily, on the first add to the source
unmodifiableList is a read-only view of live, not a copy
live.add should have thrown, but ArrayList ignores the wrapper
List.of("v1") is shared, so both lists point to the same array
explanation: Collections.unmodifiableList wraps the original list: callers cannot modify it through the wrapper, but changes made to the underlying list show through. To freeze the current contents, take a copy, for example List.copyOf(live), which is both immutable and independent.
fixNote: Used List.copyOf(live) to take a real immutable snapshot.
debugTip: Add a watch on snapshot.size() and step over line 8; it changes from 1 to 2 even though snapshot was never touched, which means it is a view.

title: Building a tag list from lookups
scenario: Two nicknames are looked up and collected into a list, where a missing one should show as null. The lookups succeed, then the program crashes.
symptom:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException
	at java.base/java.util.Objects.requireNonNull(Objects.java:208)
	at java.base/java.util.ImmutableCollections$List12.<init>(ImmutableCollections.java:563)
	at java.base/java.util.List.of(List.java:827)
	at Main.main(Main.java:11)
question: What's the root cause?
options: List.of rejects null elements, and c is null
TreeMap.get throws for keys it does not contain
println cannot print a list that contains null
List.of needs at least three elements
explanation: The immutable lists returned by List.of (and Set.of, Map.of, List.copyOf) do not allow null elements and check every argument with Objects.requireNonNull. nick.get("cat") returned null, so construction fails. The JDK frames (requireNonNull, List12.<init>, List.of) lead straight back to line 11.
fixNote: Used Arrays.asList(a, c), which accepts null elements.
debugTip: Read the trace downward past the java.base frames to the first Main frame (line 11). Break there and evaluate c == null to confirm which argument was rejected.

title: Grouping players by team gives nothing
scenario: Each row adds a player to their team's list. After the loop the map is empty, and nothing throws.
question: What's the root cause?
options: TreeMap cannot hold List values without a comparator
add(r[1]) fails silently because the list is immutable
r[0] is a copy of the key, so the map does not see it
getOrDefault returns the default without storing it in the map
explanation: getOrDefault only reads: when the key is missing it hands back the default value but never puts it into the map. Each new ArrayList receives a name and is then thrown away. computeIfAbsent both creates and stores the list when the key is absent, then returns it.
fixNote: Replaced getOrDefault with computeIfAbsent(r[0], k -> new ArrayList<>()).
debugTip: Add a watch on byTeam.size() and step through the loop: it stays 0 after every add, so the list being appended to is not the one in the map.

title: Pruning out-of-stock items crashes
scenario: Items with zero stock should be removed from the map. The program crashes on the first removal.
symptom:
Exception in thread "main" java.util.ConcurrentModificationException
	at java.base/java.util.TreeMap$PrivateEntryIterator.nextEntry(TreeMap.java:1486)
	at java.base/java.util.TreeMap$KeyIterator.next(TreeMap.java:1540)
	at Main.main(Main.java:9)
question: Which fix is correct?
options: Wrap the loop in synchronized (stock) { ... }
Call stock.keySet().remove(k) instead of stock.remove(k)
Replace the loop with stock.values().removeIf(v -> v == 0)
Switch to a HashMap, whose iterator allows removal
explanation: Removing from the map directly while iterating its keySet changes the map's modCount, so the iterator's next() throws ConcurrentModificationException. keySet().remove(k) is the same structural change and fails the same way, and synchronization is irrelevant in a single thread. Removing through the collection view's removeIf (or Iterator.remove()) is the supported way to delete during iteration.
fixNote: Replaced the loop with stock.values().removeIf(v -> v == 0).
debugTip: Set an exception breakpoint on ConcurrentModificationException, then select the Main frame (line 9) in the call stack; the TreeMap iterator frames above it show the failure is in next(), right after the removal on line 11.

title: Sorting temperatures with a tolerance
scenario: Readings within 2 degrees are treated as ties to make the sort "fuzzy". The sorted list comes out with 5 before 3.
question: What's the root cause?
options: The comparator is not transitive: 1~3 and 3~5 tie, but 1<5
Collections.sort is unstable and shuffles tied elements
Math.abs overflows for small differences
Collections.sort ignores comparators on lists of Integer
explanation: A Comparator must be transitive, including for ties: if a==b and b==c then a==c. Here 1 ties with 3 and 3 ties with 5, but 1 is less than 5, so there is no consistent order. TimSort reverses the leading run to [1, 5], then sees 3 "equal" to 5 and leaves it last. Broken comparators give garbage (or "Comparison method violates its general contract!" on larger inputs).
fixNote: Sort with a real total order (Comparator.naturalOrder()); handle tolerance separately, e.g. when grouping.
debugTip: Put a breakpoint inside the lambda on line 6 and log a, b and the result for each call; you will see compare(3, 5) return 0 while compare(1, 5) returned -1.

title: The grid walker revisits a cell
scenario: Visited cells are stored as int[] pairs. The cell {1, 2} was already visited, but the check says to visit it again.
question: What's the root cause?
options: contains only checks the last element added
contains uses equals, and arrays inherit identity equals
int[] is autoboxed to Integer[] and the boxes differ
The list must be sorted before contains can find anything
explanation: List.contains calls equals() on each element. Arrays do not override equals, so it is Object.equals, which is reference identity; next is a different array object from the stored {1, 2}. Compare contents with Arrays.equals, or store List<Integer> or a record instead of arrays.
fixNote: Check by content: visited.stream().anyMatch(p -> Arrays.equals(p, next)).
debugTip: Break on line 9 and evaluate next.equals(visited.get(0)) and Arrays.equals(next, visited.get(0)) side by side: false vs true.

title: Unsaved changes on an untouched document
scenario: An editor clones the saved data and flags the document dirty if the copy differs from the saved version. Nothing has been edited yet.
question: What does this print?
options: false, false, true
true, false, true
false, true, false
false, true, true
explanation: clone() makes a new array, so == is false. Arrays inherit Object.equals, which is also identity, so current.equals(saved) is false and dirty becomes true. Only Arrays.equals compares element by element and returns true.
fixNote: Compute dirty with !Arrays.equals(current, saved).
debugTip: Break on line 8 and evaluate current.equals(saved) and Arrays.equals(current, saved) in the debugger; when two calls that "should" agree disagree, check which equals is actually being used.

title: Formatting a tag list
scenario: Tags should be shown as [java, sql, go] and also as a pipe-separated line.
question: What does this print?
options: [java, sql, go] then java|sql|go
[java[sql[go] then java|sql|go
, java[sql[go] then java|sql|go
[java, sql, go] then |java|sql|go|
explanation: Collectors.joining takes (delimiter, prefix, suffix), in that order. Here the delimiter is "[", the prefix is ", " and the suffix is "]", giving ", java[sql[go]". String.join("|", tags) puts the separator only between elements.
fixNote: Reordered the arguments to joining(", ", "[", "]").
debugTip:
Break on line 9 and evaluate tags.stream().collect(Collectors.joining("", "

", "")) with marker strings; the result shows which argument goes where.

title: Printing a priority queue
scenario: Five numbers go into a PriorityQueue, and the author prints the queue expecting to see them in sorted order.
question: What does this print?
explanation: PriorityQueue is a binary min-heap stored in an array. It only guarantees that the head is the smallest; toString() and iteration walk the backing array in heap order. Adding 5, 1, 4, 2, 3 with sift-up leaves the array as [1, 2, 4, 5, 3]. To get sorted order, poll() repeatedly.
fixNote: Drain the queue with poll() to get elements in priority order.
debugTip: Inspect pq in the variables view after the loop and expand its internal queue array: it holds heap order, not sorted order, which is exactly what toString() prints.

title: Sorting names from a loader
scenario: Names come from a helper method and are sorted for display. The size prints, then sorting crashes.
symptom:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException
	at java.base/java.util.ImmutableCollections.uoe(ImmutableCollections.java:142)
	at java.base/java.util.ImmutableCollections$AbstractImmutableList.sort(ImmutableCollections.java:261)
	at java.base/java.util.Collections.sort(Collections.java:145)
	at Main.main(Main.java:11)
question: What's the root cause?
options: loadNames returns an immutable List.of list, which cannot be sorted in place
Collections.sort needs a Comparator for String
Strings of different lengths cannot be compared
names is a view of a temporary array that was freed
explanation: List.of returns an unmodifiable list; every mutator, including sort(), throws UnsupportedOperationException. Collections.sort(list) just calls list.sort(null), as the frames show. Reading past the JDK frames to Main line 11 tells you who tried to mutate, and the list's origin (line 5) tells you why it is immutable. Copy into an ArrayList before sorting.
fixNote: Sort a mutable copy: new ArrayList<>(loadNames()).
debugTip: Break on line 11 and evaluate names.getClass(): java.util.ImmutableCollections$ListN tells you the list is from List.of before you even step into sort().
